items.actClause: AN ACT to amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating to tickets to places of entertainment, in relation to extending the expiration of the provisions thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6444

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991, amending the arts and
cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to
the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating to tickets to places
of entertainment, in relation to extending the expiration of the
provisions thereof


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF THE BILL :
Extends provisions of law relating to ticket scalping.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
Section 1. Amends section 4 of Chapter 704 of the laws of 1991,
amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws
of 1920, as amended by chapter 68 of the laws of 2009 by extending the
date in which the law shall be in full force and effect until May 15,
2012.

Section 2. Effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :
Chapter 61 of the laws of 2007 created a shift in the way that
operators, venues, ticket brokers, and the general public could access
tickets after the primary sale. Gone were the caps imposed on what
could be charged for a ticket on the secondary market in favor of a
free market approach. During the two years of free market secondary
ticket sales, few if any complaints have surfaced on the conduct of
the secondary market. These provisions were extended by chapter 68 of
the laws of 2009 and this bill extends the current law and keeps the
secondary market intact.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.actClause: AN ACT to amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating to tickets to places of entertainment, in relation to extending the expiration of the provisions thereof
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6444A

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to
resale of tickets to places of entertainment; to amend chapter 704 of
the laws of 1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and
chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing
and wrestling relating to tickets to places of entertainment, in
relation to the effectiveness thereof


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :
This bill would ensure proper and sufficient regulation of the resale
of tickets.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :
Section 1 of the bill would amend §25.03 of the Arts and Cultural
Affairs Law to add the definition of ticket office to the current law.

Section 2 would amend §25.11 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law to
add the definition of ticket office to the section.

Section 3 would add ticket office to the buffer zone surrounding
places of entertainment.

Section 4 would make changes to the bond requirement.

Section 5 would enact the previous sections and sunset them in two
years on May 15, 2012, while making the amendments to section 25.11
permanent.

Section 6 would prohibit an operator or operator's agent to sell or
convey tickets to any secondary ticket reseller owned or controlled by
such operator or operator's agent.

Section 7 would add a new section 25.24 which would make using
automated ticket purchasing software a crime and would impose
penalties for such.

Section 8 would deem the provisions of the bill in full force and
effect from May 25, 2010 through May 25, 2011.

Section 9 would enact the bill and makes the amendments to 25.15 and
to 25.24 permanent.

 JUSTIFICATION :
In 2009 when the current regulation of ticket resale was set to
sunset, the conversation once again turned to the effectiveness of
regulation on the current market. It quickly became apparent that such
a multifaceted industry warranted an in-depth review of practices; and
problems facing both industry and consumers alike. The Department of
State was then commissioned to carry out such a review and report back
to the legislature. This legislation places regulation on the ticket
resale industry based on those findings.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
New Bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

B.actClause: AN ACT to amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating to tickets to places of entertainment, in relation to extending the expiration of the provisions thereof
B.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S6444B

TITLE OF BILL:

An act
to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to resale of
tickets to places of entertainment; to amend chapter 704 of the laws of
1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the
laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating
to tickets to places of entertainment,
in relation to the effectiveness thereof

PURPOSE:

This bill would extend the scheduled sunset of Article 25 of the Arts
and Cultural Affairs Law (ACAL), until May 15, 2011, make ACAL
25.11 permanent, and make various other changes to the law governing
ticket sales.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.03 to add a new
subdivision (10) to create the definition for a "ticket office."

Section 2 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.11 to add a new
subdivision (4) to create the definition of a "ticket office."
Section 3 of the bill would include ticket offices as locations
protected by a 1,500 foot buffer zone, inside of which tickets cannot
be resold.

Section 3 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.11 to include a ticket
office within the Scope of the buffer zone provisions set forth by
this section.

Section 4 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.15 to clarify how the
Secretary of State can draw upon bonds posted by the licensees of
Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law.

Section 5 of the bill would amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991 to
extend the effectiveness of Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural
Affairs Law.

Section 6 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.25 to require that
licensees report to the Consumer Protection Board information related
to the resale of tickets.

Section 7 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.29(1) to require that
service charges in association with tickets sold be reasonable.

Section 8 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.30 to require that
consumers be provided with the option of a transferrable ticket at
the time of first public sale.

Section 9 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.35 to add a new
subdivision (7) to allow for increases in fines for certain
violations of ACAL Article 25 when such violations are committed by
firms, corporations or entities other than individual persons.

Section 10 of the bill would create a new ACAL § 25.24 to prohibit the
use of automated ticket purchasing software.

Section 11 of the bill would make ACAL § 25.11 permanent.

Section 12 of the bill would make the bill effective immediately.

EXISTING LAW:

The regulatory framework governing the sale and resale of tickets to
places of entertainment is contained in Article 25 of the ACAL

STATEMENT IN SUPPORT:

This legislation would extend the effectiveness of ACAL Article 25 for
one year, and prevent the consequent reversion to a governance
framework contained in the presently dormant Article 25 of the Arts
and Cultural Affairs Law as promulgated generally by the Laws of
1920. The purpose of this extension is to avoid unnecessary
disruption in the ticket sale and resale marketplace, as well as the
enforcement burdens that will result from a sunset.

In addition, this legislation would enact new provisions to protect
consumers. Specifically, the bill will prohibit the use of automated
ticket purchasing software, which presently is used by unscrupulous
speculators to purchase tickets at initial sale ahead of consumers
intending to attend an event. While the use of this software is
typically banned by the policies of ticket issuers and venue
operators, this statutory prohibition would allow the State to
intervene to further protect consumers.

This legislation would also extend new consumer protections on the
primary market, by prohibiting venue operators and their agents from
employing paperless ticketing systems that do not allow consumers to
transfer their tickets independent of the operator or operator's
agent, unless the operator offers the consumer a choice of purchasing
independently transferrable tickets in another form. Additionally,
operators would be prohibited from charging higher prices based on
the form of ticket a consumer selects, and would be allowed to assess
only reasonable surcharges on other than paperless forms of tickets.

Further, the legislation would provide for a new reporting requirement
for licensees that would enable the State to better determine the

impact of the resale marketplace on consumers, as well as to study
the purchasing trends of consumers.

Finally, the bill would make permanent ACAL § 25.11, which relates to
ticket office buffer zones.

BUDGET IMPLICATIONS:

This legislation would not have any impact on the State's Financial
Plan.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act would take effect immediately, with provisions.
